translation: An act of the court should prejudice no one.
meaning: A court may correct prejudice attributable to its own procedural error, within its lawful powers.
example: A litigant follows an erroneous deposit direction issued by court staff and seeks restoration when the error is discovered.
caution: Not a general excuse for a party's own negligence or a power to disregard every statutory deadline.

sources.title: Jang Singh v. Brijlal (1963)
sources.pinpoint: Discussion of the erroneous deposit and court-caused prejudice.

meaning: A person affected by a decision should ordinarily have a meaningful opportunity to respond to adverse material.
example: Before cancelling a licence, an authority ordinarily provides notice of the allegations and a fair opportunity to respond.
caution: The content of a hearing depends on the statutory context; exceptions and prejudice require examination.

sources.title: Satyavir Singh v. Union of India (1985)

meaning: A person entrusted with statutory power ordinarily cannot transfer that decision-making power without authority.
example: An officer given power to decide a licence application cannot simply assign the final decision to a clerk without legal authority.
caution: Express or implied authorization may permit subdelegation; ministerial assistance differs from transfer of discretion.

sources.title: Sidhartha Sarawgi v. Board of Trustees for Port of Kolkata (2014)
sources.pinpoint: Discussion under Delegatus Non Potest Delegare.

meaning: General words following specific words may be confined to an identifiable common class where the context warrants.
example: A rule covering cars, buses, trucks and other vehicles may be read as addressing road vehicles if the context supports that class.
caution: There must be an identifiable genus and no contrary legislative intention; the canon is not mandatory.

sources.title: Amar Chandra Chakraborty v. Collector of Excise (1972)
sources.pinpoint: Discussion of the conditions for ejusdem generis.

term: Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus
translation: False in one thing, false in everything.
meaning: The maxim proposes rejecting all testimony because part is false. Indian criminal courts do not apply it as a mandatory rule.
example: A witness exaggerates one incident; the court assesses whether other parts of the evidence are independently credible.
caution: Do not use the maxim as an automatic ground to discard all evidence. Reliable and unreliable portions may sometimes be separated.

sources.title: Ugar Ahir v. State of Bihar (1964)
sources.pinpoint: Discussion rejecting the maxim as a rule of law or practice.

translation: The law does not compel the impossible.
meaning: Genuine impossibility may be relevant when interpreting or applying an obligation, depending on the legal framework.
example: Compliance requires an act that has become objectively impossible through circumstances outside the obligated party's control.
caution: Difficulty, expense or self-created obstacles are not necessarily impossibility; the applicable legislation controls.

sources.title: Narmada Bachao Andolan v. State of M.P. (2011)
sources.pinpoint: Discussion of impossibility and the scope of the doctrine.

translation: No one should judge their own cause.
meaning: Decision-makers should be free from legally disqualifying bias or conflicting interests.
example: A member of a disciplinary panel has a personal financial interest in the outcome of the inquiry.
caution: The applicable bias test and doctrines such as necessity depend on the facts and legal framework.
aliases: Nemo debet esse judex in propria causa

sources.title: Satyavir Singh v. Union of India (1985)

translation: A word is known by its associates.
meaning: The meaning of a potentially ambiguous expression may be informed by the surrounding words.
example: The word 'paper' in a list of industrial packaging materials may take meaning from the neighbouring items, if the context warrants.
caution: Context cannot override clear statutory language or an evident intention to give a word broader scope.

sources.title: Rohit Pulp and Paper Mills Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise (1990)

meaning: In an appropriate negligence case, proved circumstances may support an inference of negligence without direct proof of the precise negligent act.
example: An object falls from equipment under a defendant's management in circumstances that ordinarily would not occur with proper care.
caution: Not strict liability or automatic proof of criminal guilt; the evidential context and explanations matter.

sources.title: Syad Akbar v. State of Karnataka (1979)
sources.pinpoint: Discussion of the evidentiary function and criminal negligence.

meaning: Section 11 CPC restricts re-litigation of issues that meet its requirements, including prior final determination by a competent court.
example: The same parties attempt to litigate an ownership issue already finally determined between them under the same title.
caution: The statutory conditions and explanations must be examined; not every dismissal or earlier observation bars a later case.

translation: Where there is a right, there is a remedy.
meaning: A legally recognized right ordinarily calls for a means of enforcement or redress.
example: A person whose enforceable civil right is infringed seeks the remedy provided by the relevant law.
caution: The maxim does not create a remedy outside statutory jurisdiction or override procedural bars.
